text: Reference data is 'stable,' but it isn't static. This lesson covers the lifecycle a code list actually goes through: add, deprecate, retire.

Codes get added when a new valid value is needed. Codes get deprecated when they shouldn't be used for new records, but old records still reference them. The single most important idea here: deprecated is not the same as deleted.

Delete a code outright, and every historical record that referenced it points at nothing — a report against last year's orders breaks or silently drops rows. Deprecating a code, marking it inactive while keeping the row for old records, is almost always the right move.

A well-designed code table carries an effective-from and effective-to date. Here, 'PEND' was retired mid-2023 in favor of 'RVW' — but it's still in the table, marked inactive, so any order placed before July 2023 still resolves to a real row instead of a broken reference.

Nobody edits a code list directly in production. Every list needs a defined owner, a documented reason for each change, and a predictable release process — the same rigor applied to a typo in a reference table as to a bug in application code.
Next lesson: reference data governance in full — who owns these lists, and how a change actually gets approved.
